a: A clear role and task, relevant context clearly delimited, explicit constraints (answer only from context, say "I don't know"), a few examples of the exact format, and a defined output schema. Then test it on an evaluation set and iterate.

Zero-shot: instructions only. Few-shot: include examples so the model copies the pattern (in-context learning). Chain-of-thought: ask for step-by-step reasoning before the answer, which helps multi-step problems at the cost of more tokens.

q: What is prompt injection and how do you defend against it?
a: Instructions hidden in user input or retrieved content that try to override the system prompt or trigger tools. Defences: treat retrieved/user content as data with clear delimiters, input/output classifiers, least-privilege tools, human approval for risky actions, never placing secrets in prompts, and monitoring.

q: How do you manage prompts in production?
a: Version them like code, keep them out of hard-coded strings (templates/config), evaluate every change against a golden test set, log which prompt version produced each answer, and A/B test significant changes.

q: What is chain-of-thought and when does it hurt?
a: Asking the model to reason step by step before answering; it helps multi-step maths and logic. It adds tokens (cost, latency), may not help simple lookups, and adds little or can hurt with reasoning models that already think internally.
Sample several chain-of-thought answers at higher temperature and take the majority final answer. Improves accuracy on reasoning tasks at the cost of several calls.

Malicious instructions hidden in content the system retrieves or a tool returns (a web page, email, PDF), not typed by the user. Especially dangerous for RAG and agents with tools. Defend with content separation, least-privilege tools, output validation and human approval for actions.

q: How do you test whether a prompt change is an improvement?
a: Run old and new prompts on the same frozen evaluation set, compare task metrics (accuracy, faithfulness, format validity), read the failures, change one thing at a time, and only then ship, ideally via A/B test.

q: Few-shot examples: how many and which?
a: Typically 2–5, covering edge cases and all labels in balance, in the exact output format. Test 0/3/5 on the eval set: more examples cost tokens and can bias the model towards the most common label.
